The Food Safety Officer (FSO) is empowered to take samples of any article of food, inspect any food business premises, and seize articles that appear to be unsafe, misbranded or sub-standard; the powers are defined under s37 (and sampling under s38/s41).

add_notes.When taking a food sample the Food Safet: v1 enumerated one particular procedural sequence; answer covered the same safeguards (witnesses, custody, cost, analysis, reporting) with different wording.

When taking a food sample the Food Safety Officer must follow the prescribed procedure - draw the sample in the presence of a witness, divide and seal/code the parts, deliver one part to the Food Analyst for analysis, and follow the notice-and-custody safeguards that make the process fair and transparent.

add_notes.The Food Analyst's role is not limited t: v1 framed the Food Analyst only as certifying FSO samples; it omitted the purchaser-analysis route, notified laboratories and the contravention forwarding step.

The Food Analyst's role is not limited to samples sent by a Food Safety Officer: any purchaser of an article of food may have it analysed by the Food Analyst on payment of fees and receive the report of analysis within the regulatory period, accredited laboratories are notified by the Food Authority to carry out such analysis, and a report finding contravention is forwarded onward for prosecution.

conclusions: A prohibition order prohibits the FBO from using premises or a process/equipment for food handling where there is a risk to public safety; failure to comply attracts penalties. It operates alongside improvement and emergency prohibition notices.

Section 33 should be read as a judicial restriction with consequences tied to the scope of the order, rather than as another name for an improvement notice or an emergency administrative direction. Its application can extend beyond one item of equipment to the relevant food-business activity or class, and the statutory scheme contemplates a route for seeking discharge after corrective measures are evidenced. The reference should therefore recognize the order’s court-based character, its potential management restriction, and the remedial pathway as distinct legal effects.

Carrying on a food business without a licence is punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to six months and a fine which may extend to five lakh rupees.

Sub-standard food (s60) and misbranded food (s61) attract a fine (s60 up to 5 lakh, s61 up to 3 lakh); misleading advertisement (s53) is a separate offence carrying a fine (the 2020 amendment raised it to 10 lakh) and applies to the person responsible for the advertisement.

Any person aware of, or suspecting, a notifiable disease in animals must report it promptly to the competent veterinary authority / District Animal Husbandry Officer under the WB infectious-diseases rules.

add_notes.Under s3(1) of the Environment (Protecti: Answer stated the broad s3(1) power accurately; v1's narrower 'threatened' phrasing depressed overlap.

conclusions: Under s3, when the Central Government is satisfied that the whole or any part of India's environment is threatened, it may take such measures as it deems necessary or expedient for protecting the environment.

Under s3(1) of the Environment (Protection) Act 1986 the Central Government may take all such measures as it deems necessary or expedient for protecting and improving the quality of the environment and preventing environmental pollution, exercising the power when it is satisfied that substantial environmental threat exists.

Every occupier who proposes to discharge, or is discharging, effluent must obtain prior consent to establish and consent to operate from the State Pollution Control Board (or CPCB) under s9 of the Water Act.

No person shall establish or operate an industrial installation handling any toxic/foreign substance without prior consent from the State Pollution Board; operating without consent is ground for closure under s7.

Under s6, the Central Government may, in a case of environmental emergency or where standards are being violated, direct the closure and/or demolition of the industry, and may also empower a State Government or Pollution Board to take the same action.

Under s7, the Boards may, after recording reasons and giving the occupier a chance, close or regulate the pipe/continuous supply and may require the occupier to stop the polluting process, besides inspecting and accessing records.

Before passing a closure/demolition order under s6 the authority must give the industry a reasonable opportunity of being heard (show-cause), except where it is satisfied that in an environmental emergency there is insufficient time to do so.

Contravention of an order under the Water Act is punishable with imprisonment up to 3 months (5 months for subsequent convictions) and a fine of at least 2000 rupees per day for continuing offences, and is cognizable.

Section 7 makes it an offence to contravene any rule or order made under the EPA; the offence is cognizable and punishable with imprisonment up to 5 years and a fine which may extend to 1 lakh rupees.

conclusions: The Boards are duty-bound under the EPA framework to lay and enforce environmental (including water-quality) standards notified under s8 of the Water Act, monitoring compliance with the notified ambient/effluent standards.

Within the EPA framework the standard-setting function covers laying down standards for the quality of environment and for emission or discharge of environmental pollutants from any source, which is how the water-quality intersection works: Board duties to enforce notified ambient and effluent standards operate under standards laid down through this power and under the Water Act s8 notifications.

Consent is administered by the State Board, which inspects sewage and trade effluents, works and plants and reviews plans and specifications in connection with the grant of any consent required by the Act; running a prescribed process without that consent or without complying with its conditions is a breach by the occupier that the Board may act on.

The FBO must segregate waste at source into biodegradable/recyclable/dry and hand it over only to the municipal door-to-door collector; open dumping is prohibited. The municipal/Urban Local Body is responsible for door-to-door collection and processing.

An environmentally sensitive area is one notified by the Central Government where it proposes to restrict any process/activity that may or is likely to cause environmental quality deterioration; s5 empowers restrictions on use of such areas/substrates.

Criminal proceedings under s7 may be instituted by the Central Government or an officer authorised by it, before a Magistrate of the first class; prosecution of a government servant requires the previous sanction of the Central Government under s8.

conclusions: A wholesale meat/fish market requires both a municipal market licence under the KMC Act and a licence under the West Bengal Meat Order; the two regimes apply cumulatively and neither substitutes the other.

The KMC permission framework also contains a sequencing rule: where another government or statutory body must authorize the proposed use, the Corporation ordinarily requires that permission before granting its own permission. The supplied text recognizes a limited provisional-permission route when municipal permission is itself a precondition for the external authorization; that provisional permission is confined to satisfying the precondition and becomes final only after the other permission is produced. This procedural qualification supplements, rather than replaces, the separate market and meat-trade authorizations.

add_notes.Providing sewerage and drainage, constru: v1 bundled drainage and nuisance removal together; it did not identify the specific obligatory-function clauses that ground the duty and the resulting order power.

conclusions: The Corporation must maintain drainage/sewerage and may prohibit/order the removal of noxious liquid discharge or other nuisances harmful to public health, under its municipal nuisance powers.

Providing sewerage and drainage, constructing and cleansing sewers and drains, and the scavenging and removal of filth and obnoxious matters are obligatory functions of the Corporation, and those functions support orders against noxious liquid discharge and other nuisances harmful to public health.

add_notes.Where the Municipal Commissioner is of t: v1 spoke generally of trade/licensing provisions; the operative ground is the s517 notice power and who may be served with it.

conclusions: The Municipal Commissioner may require removal of encroachments/unauthorised stalls and regulate signage where they cause obstruction or public nuisance, under the KMC trade/licensing provisions.

Where the Municipal Commissioner is of the opinion that a nuisance exists on any land or building, section 517 lets him require the person whose act, default or sufferance caused or continued it, or the owner, lessee or occupier, to remove or abate the nuisance within the period specified in the written notice, which reaches obstructive stalls, signage and similar street nuisances.

add_notes.The nuisance process is not best represe: The audited answers correctly identify nuisance abatement and the written-notice route. conclusions: The owner must keep premises free of nuisances and dispose waste per the KMC sanitation rules; failure invites a notice/civic penalty and removal of the nuisance by the Corporation, with costs recovered as a civic due.

The nuisance process is not best represented as an automatic fixed fine triggered solely by the presence of flies. The statutory route described in the packet is directed first at securing removal or abatement, with municipal intervention available where the nuisance is not dealt with; any recovery of the Corporation’s abatement expense is a separate consequence from the initial notice. The gold reference should preserve this notice-and-remedy sequence and avoid asserting a specific monetary amount or compliance period that the supplied excerpts do not establish.

The Corporation may recover water/fees and property-tax dues through the civic dues recovery mechanism (including recovery from other sources); water supply may be disconnected for non-payment of water charges.

add_notes.Erection, re-erection or extension of a: v1 stated the prohibition and a possible pull-down order; widened to the penalty structure recorded for s392 contravention.

conclusions: Building work without sanction is prohibited under s392; the Corporation may impose penalty and/or pass an order requiring the unauthorised structure to be pulled down/regularised after due procedure.

Erection, re-erection or extension of a building in Kolkata requires the prior sanction of the Municipal Commissioner, and carrying out building work without that sanction contravenes section 392 of the KMC Act, 1980, which attracts the prescribed penalty of imprisonment and/or fine computed per building and per square metre, with a further penalty where the unauthorised construction or execution of work is continued.

The hotel must obtain a municipal fire-safety NOC and the KMC may make the trade licence subject to fire-safety compliance; the two clearances are co-ordinated and the licence may be conditioned on the NOC.

add_notes.Where a removal notice is not complied w: v1 stated cost recovery abstractly; it missed the self-execution power and the arrear-of-tax recovery route that makes the cost enforceable.

conclusions: The Commissioner may remove an obstruction from a public place and recover the cost from the owner as a municipal (civic) due recoverable under the KMC recovery provisions.

Where a removal notice is not complied with, the Commissioner may himself carry out the removal after the notice period expires and recover the expenses from the owner as an arrear of tax under the Act, so obstruction removal from a public place carries a cost recovery enforceable exactly like a municipal due.
Section 30 prohibits sub-letting or assigning premises without the prior permission of the landlord (and the prescribed authority); permission is required before any sub-letting.

add_notes.Under section 16 of the West Bengal Prem: v1 referred to 'the procedure in s16, comparable premises and the Act's factors' — the 1956 Act's approach; widened to the actual s16 computation in the 1997 Act.

conclusions: The standard rent is determined by the prescribed authority (Rent Controller) in accordance with the procedure in s16, based on comparable premises and the Act's factors.

Under section 16 of the West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act, 1997 the fair rent is determined by applying the section's tenure-based formulae rather than a single figure: for premises constructed and let out after 1984 it is ten per cent of the cost of construction plus the market value of the land at the commencement of construction; for premises constructed on or before 1984 it is the recorded rent as on 1.7.1976 where the tenancy subsists for twenty years or more, or as on 1.7.1986 where it subsists for ten to twenty years, increased by not more than three times or two times respectively and then adjusted by the deductions in Schedule III.
Enhanced rent may exceed standard rent only for premises the tenant has improved (up to the improvement value); the enhancement procedure is governed by s32 and requires authority fixation.

The landlord must give the tenant a notice (specifying grounds and reasonable time to show cause) before instituting eviction proceedings; eviction is on grounds listed in s45 (e.g. non-payment of rent, sub-letting without permission).

After an eviction decree, s46 provides for recovery of possession through the court's execution process (including removal of the tenant by the local authority if necessary), subject to procedural safeguards.
Under s3 of the EPA, the Central Government may take such measures as it deems necessary or expedient to protect and improve the quality of the environment, including drinking-water sources.

Section 8 empowers the CPCB to notify the quality of water (including standards for surface water used or intended for drinking) and of effluents; compliance with those notified standards is mandatory.

add_notes.The institutional allocation matters as: The audit missed an institutional qualification in the supplied s6 text. This addition broadens the accepted account of Board powers by recording which Board acts in Union territories, without merely repeating the listed substantive powers.

conclusions: Under s6, the Boards may take steps for the prevention, control and abatement of air pollution, including notifying ambient air-quality and emission standards to protect public health.

The institutional allocation matters as well as the substantive pollution-control powers: for a Union territory, the Act assigns the Central Board the functions that a State Board would otherwise perform, rather than requiring a separate State Board to be constituted there. This jurisdictional substitution is part of the statutory machinery through which the Act’s standards and control functions operate, and is a valid additional dimension of the public-protection answer.

Consent to operate under s9 is granted subject to the condition that the effluent shall not exceed the notified effluent standards, thereby protecting the quality of water used (downstream) for drinking.

Locating a polluting industry in an environmentally sensitive area (s2(e), notified to protect public health/environment) triggers s5 restrictions on the use of land/substrate and may bar the activity or require extra safeguards.

Generators must segregate waste at source (biodegradable/recyclable/dry) and hand it over only to the ULBs' door-to-door collectors; proper segregation prevents open dumping/burning that harms public health.

add_notes.The amendment empowers notification proh: v1 combined prohibition and EPR in one sentence; it missed that the restriction operates by notification over the enumerated commodity classes.

conclusions: The amended PWM Rules prohibit the manufacture/import/sale of notified single-use plastic items; EPR makes the producer responsible for the plastic's end-of-life, reducing public-health exposure to littered plastic.

The amendment empowers notification prohibiting manufacture, import, stocking, distribution, sale and use of carry bags, plastic sheets, multilayered packaging and single-use plastic including polystyrene and expanded polystyrene commodities, with extended producer responsibility duties on producers, importers and brand-owners for end-of-life management so that littered plastic exposure falls off.

Discharging polluted water in contravention of an order is an offence punishable with imprisonment up to 3 months (5 months on subsequent conviction) and a fine of at least 2000 rupees/day; untreated discharge also raises public-health exposure.

The plant must obtain environmental/public-health clearance under the EPA (and the Water Act consent regime) given proximity to a drinking-water source; clearance is not automatic and may impose conditions or prohibit the location (s3/s6).

add_notes.The Act’s contents identify separate mec: The machine failed to credit the evidentiary distinction between the Act’s framework powers and a technical ambient standard. The addition specifies why a numerical limit requires the relevant standard text and averaging period, not just the Act’s general powers.

conclusions: The available corpus does not establish the specific numeric PM2.5 24-hour ambient standard as readable from the Act text itself; ambient air-quality criteria are notified by the CPCB over time and the exact figure is not established in the corpus.

The Act’s contents identify separate mechanisms for declaring air-pollution-control areas and for regulating emissions, but those are enabling and regulatory mechanisms, not a numeric table of ambient PM2.5 concentrations. A claim about a 24-hour particulate limit therefore needs the applicable notified standard and its units/averaging period; a general reference to Board powers cannot itself supply the numerical value or establish that value as wording in the Act.

add_notes.Under s73 a party injured by breach is c: Answer's s73/s74 distinction was substantively sound; v1's 'disallowed to the extent of penalty' phrasing diverged.

conclusions: s73 gives compensation for loss actually suffered from a breach; a 'penalty' clause promising a lump-sum irrespective of actual loss is not enforceable as compensation (s74) and is disallowed to the extent of penalty.

Under s73 a party injured by breach is compensated only for loss actually suffered and arising naturally in the usual course of things or within the parties' contemplation; a stipulated sum by way of penalty is governed by s74, under which only reasonable compensation not exceeding the stipulated amount may be recovered rather than the full penalty sum.

add_notes.Under the Sale of Goods Act, 1930 the pa: v1 gave the ascertained/unascertained rule only; widened to the full s20–s23 sequence so the timing rules read together.

conclusions: Ownership and risk pass when the goods are ascertained and the contract is made (s16); for unascertained goods, risk passes only when the goods are ascertained and the property is intended to pass, per the Act's general rules.

Under the Sale of Goods Act, 1930 the passing of property — and with it the risk — is governed by the state of the goods: for specific goods under an unconditional contract in a deliverable state the property passes when the contract is made; where the seller must first put the goods into a deliverable state, or weigh, measure or test them to ascertain the price, the property passes only when that act is done and the buyer has notice; and for unascertained or future goods by description the property passes only when goods of that description in a deliverable state are unconditionally appropriated to the contract with the assent of the other party.

add_notes.A partner's act done in the ordinary cou: Answer covered implied authority and contractual limits; v1's s22/s30 section anchoring depressed overlap.

conclusions: An act done by a partner in the ordinary course of the firm's business binds the firm and the partners (s22); the authority is implied (s30) for acts usual in the business, but not for acts outside the ordinary course.

A partner's act done in the ordinary course of the firm's business binds the firm and the partners; the authority is implied for acts usual in such business, mutual agency can be restricted by agreement between partners, but restrictions do not affect third parties without notice.

A related party transaction requires prior approval by special resolution (and, for material transactions, approval of the Audit Committee and members); ordinary resolution applies only where the audit committee/company is authorised to deal with non-material matters.
A suit for recovery of possession of immovable property must be filed within 12 years, while a suit for breach of contract must be filed within 3 years (first schedule to the Limitation Act, 1963).

Under Part XII of the CPA 2019, the manufacturer, service provider or seller is liable to pay damages for any harm/loss/injury caused by a defective product, without the consumer needing to prove fault, subject to conditions in the Act.

Specific performance is granted at the court's discretion where compensation is an inadequate remedy; it is NOT discretionary (must be granted) for agreements to transfer an interest in immovable property, subject to the statutory bars.

The available corpus does not establish the complete, authoritatively enumerated list of strategic powers reserved to the full Board under Companies Act s179(1) that may not be delegated; the exhaustive list is set by the relevant regulation and is not firmly established in the Act text alone.

add_notes.A liquidated-damages clause naming a sum: Answer's formulation is MORE legally precise than v1 (reasonable compensation up to ceiling); v1 is retained as an alternative.

conclusions: Such a clause is treated as a penalty and is not enforceable as liquidated damages; the Act allows recovery only of the amount of loss actually proved (s73), and the court may reduce the stipulated sum to the extent it is a penalty.

A liquidated-damages clause naming a sum far exceeding probable loss is treated as a penalty; under s74 the court may award only reasonable compensation not exceeding the amount so named, the claimant proving actual loss under s73, so recovery beyond proved loss is not automatic.

An agreement without consideration is not enforceable, EXCEPT for promises made under special contracts e.g. a promise by a supplier to supply goods at a prevailing price under a written agreement, or a promise to compensate for a wrong already suffered.

add_notes.Yes - an FSSAI food licence and a munici: Answer stated the cumulative-regimes conclusion; v1's 'why' clause diluted coverage.

conclusions: Yes - the restaurant needs both a municipal trade licence (KMC Act) and an FSSAI food licence (FSS Act); the municipal trade licence and the FSSAI licence govern different statutory requirements and both apply cumulatively.

Yes - an FSSAI food licence and a municipal (KMC) trade licence are cumulative: they arise under separate statutory regimes governing different requirements, and holding one does not exempt the restaurant from the other.

The KMC Municipal Commissioner sanctions the building plan (s392) for structural/fire/waste, while the Designated Officer/FSSAI approves the food-safety layout under the FSS Act; both clearances are mandatory before operation.

add_notes.Operating without a KMC trade licence in: Answer separated the regimes correctly; token overlap with v1 fell just under threshold.

concepts: FSSAI no defence to municipal licensing
conclusions: Operating without a KMC trade licence invites municipal penalty/closure regardless of an FSSAI food licence; FSSAI registration does not exempt the vendor from the municipal trade-licensing requirement.

Operating without a KMC trade licence invites municipal penalty or closure under the KMC Act, and a valid FSSAI food licence does not exempt the vendor from the separate municipal trade-licensing requirement.

FSSAI may pass a prohibition order (s33) over unsafe food; KMC acts under its nuisance/closure powers (nuisance chapter). Both may act independently, but on a single incident each applies its own statutory closure ground.
KMC s313 links building sanction to a conformant water-supply plan, and the FSS food regulations require safe drinking water (incl. dedicated hand-washing water); the eatery must satisfy both.

add_notes.Prosecution for an offence under the FSS: v1 asserted 'separate statutes, neither bars the other'; widened to the statutory basis (s42 procedure) that makes municipal closure irrelevant to food-safety prosecution.

conclusions: Yes - KMC's closure (building) and FSSAI's prosecution (food safety) are under separate statutes; neither bars the other. FSSAI may prosecute for unsafe food (s42) even while KMC enforces building laws.

Prosecution for an offence under the FSS Act, 2006 proceeds under section 42 on the Designated Officer's decision after the Food Analyst's report and the Commissioner of Food Safety's communication, with the procedures of the Code of Criminal Procedure applying to actions taken by the Food Safety Officer; because that procedure is governed by the FSS Act, a closure or demolition order passed by the KMC under the KMC Act, 1980 neither bars nor stays a food-safety prosecution in respect of unsafe food at the same premises.
Two distinct statutory offences: a municipal offence (waste dumping under the KMC nuisance/trade provisions) and an FSS Act offence (mislabelling of pre-packed food under the labelling regulations).

add_notes.The butcher's shop must hold both an FSS: Two-licence conclusion matched; Meat Order clause numbering in the answer differed from v1's anchoring.

conclusions: The shop must hold an FSSAI food licence (FSS Act, s31) AND a licence under the West Bengal Meat Order (Order 6) to retail meat; both are mandatory and neither is a substitute for the other.

The butcher's shop must hold both an FSSAI food licence under the FSS Act s31 and a licence under the West Bengal Meat Order for retailing meat; both are mandatory and neither substitutes for the other.

The slaughter house must comply with FSS hygiene/sanitation regulations (enforced by FSSAI) and remain a licenced slaughter house under Meat Order 5 (enforced by the licensing authority); both standards apply.

EPA s6 authorises closure/demolition for environmental emergency/pollution; FSSAI may separately pass a prohibition order (s33) over unsafe food, and the Meat Order licensing authority may act on unlicensed slaughter; each regime is independent.

Pre-packed canned meat must bear FSS labelling (FSS labelling regulations) AND must originate from a licensed slaughter house (Meat Order 5) so the source is traceable; labelling without licensed sourcing is non-conforming.

The transport vehicle must be cleaned/chilled per FSS food-safety regulations, and the transport operator must hold a Meat-Order licence (Order 6) - both are required, and non-compliance is an offence under each regime.

add_notes.A licence under the West Bengal Meat Ord: v1 framed the consequence as s63; widened to the licence prohibition itself, which is the operative bar on selling after lapse.

conclusions: No - selling food (including meat) requires a valid FSSAI licence; a lapsed FSSAI licence means the shop cannot legally sell, even with a valid Meat-Order licence, and FSSAI may take action for operating without a licence (s63).

A licence under the West Bengal Meat Order, 1966 does not authorise carrying on a food business: section 31(1) of the FSS Act, 2006 prohibits any person from commencing or carrying on any food business except under a licence granted under section 31, so an operator whose FSSAI licence has lapsed may not lawfully continue to sell meat, and continued trading is a contravention of section 31 attracting the penalty prescribed for it irrespective of the Meat-Order sanction.

add_notes.Under the WB Meat Order no person may sl: v1 asserted the FSSAI point alone; it did not state the general prohibition, notified prohibited days and notification-only exemptions that make the licence distinction follow.

concepts: Food Act does not override Meat Order
conclusions: Order 4 prohibits buffalo-calf slaughter regardless of FSSAI authorisation; a valid FSSAI food licence does NOT authorise slaughter of a prohibited animal under the Meat Order, and the Meat-Order licence must be refused/refused renewal.

Under the WB Meat Order no person may slaughter any animal at a slaughter house or any other place except as the Order permits, with prohibited days such as every Thursday notified by the State Government and exemptions granted only by notification, so a separate Meat Order authority is needed and an FSSAI food licence does not authorise slaughter the Meat Order prohibits.

The rendering unit must ensure meat waste comes from FSS-compliant sources (FSSAI) and that diseased/animal-waste inputs are handled per the infectious-disease / Diseases of Animals rules (enforced by veterinary/licensing authority); EPA may also regulate emissions.

EPA s6 authorises closure/demolition for water-pollution emergencies; separately, the plant owes an FSS duty (s26) to ensure its food output is safe; the two duties are independent and both enforceable.

Four regimes apply cumulatively: the FSS Act (s31 food licence), the KMC Act (trade licence + s313 water plan), public-health rules (safe water/potability), and the Premises Tenancy Act (s30 - no sub-let without permission).

On an animal-disease alert, the veterinary/licensing authority may order stamping-out/slaughter stoppage (disease rules) and FSSAI may order food-product recall (s33) over safety; EPA may add environmental conditions - all independently.

add_notes.Section 3 is framed as an enabling power: The audit accepted the refusal to treat 500 m as established. The addition identifies the documentary bridge needed to turn broad statutory powers into an enforceable site-specific distance and distinguishes delegation from the substantive setback rule.

conclusions: The available corpus (EPA + Water Act) does not establish the 500 m setback as a determinate rule textually; the distance is fixed by notified EIA/coastal-regulation standards outside the Act corpus, and no firm figure is reliably established in the corpus.

Section 3 is framed as an enabling power to take environmental-protection measures, and the supplied text also contemplates delegation through an Official Gazette notification subject to stated limits. Neither feature, standing alone, identifies a river-specific buffer distance. A legally firm 500 m requirement would need a traceable rule, notification, consent condition, or other operative instrument that actually prescribes that distance for the relevant location and activity; a general environmental mandate is not a substitute for that instrument.

add_notes.The three regimes operate concurrently a: v1 listed three authorities with statutory hooks; widened to the operative powers of each regime as they appear in the evidence.

conclusions: Three authorities may act: the licensing authority (Meat Order s5/s6), FSSAI (s33 over non-conforming food), and EPA/CPCB (s6 water-pollution closure). No regime pre-empts another; concurrent, independent liability.

The three regimes operate concurrently and none pre-empts the others: under the FSS Act, 2006 a prohibition order may be issued under section 33, a copy affixed at the premises and knowing contravention punished with a fine extending to three lakh rupees; the West Bengal Meat Order, 1966 independently empowers its authority to require information from, and to seize articles from, a slaughter house; and the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 with its Rules sets the emission and effluent standards enforceable through the pollution-control machinery for the untreated discharge.

add_notes.Section 37 of the FSS Act, 2006 constitu: v1 asserted both may attend; widened to the separate statutory source of each inspection power (s37 FSS; municipal health and licence powers).

conclusions: Under s37 an FSO may enter and inspect for FSS compliance; the KMC Health Officer inspects under the trade licence for municipal hygiene. Both may attend, each under their own statutory power, and neither bars the other.

Section 37 of the FSS Act, 2006 constitutes Food Safety Officers with duties entrusted by the Commissioner of Food Safety, so a Government Food Safety Officer may enter and inspect the restaurant for compliance with the FSS Act and the regulations made under it; the municipal health machinery inspects separately under the KMC Act for sanitary conditions and conformity with the municipal licence, so both officers may attend the complaint visit, each acting under her own statute and neither displacing the other.

The FSSAI Central Licensing Authority issues the FSS import clearance (FSS Act s25/s31), while the KMC registers the trade for municipal purposes; the two clearances are issued by different authorities and both are required.

FSSAI prosecution requires the written approval of the Commissioner of Food Safety (s42); a KMC trade-licence prosecution is launched by/may be conducted by the KMC on behalf of the Corporation under municipal procedure.

Closure may be ordered by (a) EPA (s6) for the environmental emergency, (b) FSSAI Designated Officer (s33) for unsafe food, and (c) KMC Municipal Commissioner (s392/nuisance) for unlicensed operation — each under its own provision.

The FSO functions under the Designated Officer (who is responsible for the area), ultimately to the Commissioner of Food Safety; a KMC health inspector reports to the Municipal Commissioner - parallel hierarchies, separate Acts.

CPCB has primary jurisdiction for pollution of an inter-State river (Ganga) under the EPA/Water Act; State Board handles intra-State; FSSAI retains its independent duty (s26) over the food output - the two do not merge.

The 2020 amendment to the FSS Rules raised the minimum fine for misleading advertisements under s53 (previously lower); the current minimum fine for an advertiser is ten lakh rupees (post the 2020 amendment).

add_notes.The text of section 7 addresses the subs: The audit correctly treated the proposed higher penalty as unproven. The addition clarifies that the supplied s7 text concerns compliance with prescribed pollutant standards, so it cannot serve as evidence of a changed monetary cap.

conclusions: The available corpus does not reliably establish that the EPA s7 monetary penalty has been amended to a figure higher than one lakh rupees; whether a later amendment raised it above one lakh is not established in the corpus.

The text of section 7 addresses the substantive ceiling on pollutant release by reference to standards prescribed elsewhere; it is not, in the excerpt supplied, a monetary-penalty provision. Accordingly, the existence of a duty to comply with prescribed emission or discharge standards cannot establish that the section 7 penalty was amended to a particular amount. An amendment claim about money requires the operative penalty section or amending instrument, not the standards clause alone.

Section 3 confers power to take measures for environmental protection (and to make rules); the Act was framed under Article 253 (Parliament's power to implement international agreements), enacted in 1986 after Bhopal.

The PWM Rules (as originally notified) phased in the single-use plastic prohibition; the August 2022 amendment introduced a timeline/exemption for MSMEs (small enterprises) for certain single-use items, deferring their compliance.

add_notes.Section 188 of the Companies Act, 2013 s: v1 stated only that the 2013 Act 'tightened' approval; widened to the operative particulars-and-resolution requirements in s188.

conclusions: The 2013 Act (s188) tightened the approval regime for related-party transactions (requiring member/Board/Audit-Committee approval) versus the 1956 Act; a related-party supply contract needs special resolution if it exceeds the threshold.

Section 188 of the Companies Act, 2013 subjects a related-party supply contract to an approval and disclosure regime materially tighter than under the Companies Act, 1956: the particulars of the contract or arrangement with related parties referred to in sub-section (1) must be recorded in the prescribed form, prior approval of the company by resolution is required before entering into it, and a related party interested in the transaction may not vote on the resolution approving it, with penalties prescribed for contravention.

add_notes.The legislative extracts shown for secti: The answer’s abstention is sound, and the audit missed a useful category distinction: penalty/compounding provisions are not the fee schedule. The excerpt does not provide the medium-restaurant Type-B fee entry needed for a precise amount.

conclusions: The available corpus does not establish the exact annual licence fee for a State (Type B) food licence for a medium restaurant; the FSSAI fee rules set varying fees by category, and the precise amount for this category is not reliably established in the corpus.

The legislative extracts shown for section 31 include penalty-adjudication and compounding machinery, but those provisions answer how certain contraventions may be processed, not the annual charge for issuing a licence to a particular restaurant category. A fee answer must be tied to the applicable licensing-fee schedule and the category-specific entry in force for the relevant period. General penalty figures or procedural provisions should not be repurposed as an annual licence fee.

add_notes.Section 391’s supplied text establishes: The machine missed the distinction between the statutory body/process and the separate schedule fixing charges. The added reading records what s391 affirmatively establishes while avoiding an invented fee figure.

conclusions: The available corpus does not establish the exact schedule of building-plan scrutiny/redevelopment fees under the KMC Act; the fee structure is notified over time and the precise amounts are not reliably established in the corpus.

Section 391’s supplied text establishes a Municipal Building Committee and assigns it a scrutiny role for applications concerning erection or re-erection of buildings. That procedural allocation does not itself state a monetary tariff, rate basis, or redevelopment-fee calculation. The presence of a statutory scrutiny duty therefore supports the existence of a review process, but the amount payable must be established from the applicable rules, regulations, or fee notification rather than inferred from the committee provision.

add_notes.The excerpts under section 31 do not sup: The audit missed the distinction between the Act’s licensing framework and the regulatory classification table needed to answer the numerical question. The added reading explains why penalty-related amendments in the supplied extracts cannot establish the turnover threshold.

conclusions: The available corpus does not establish a single, stable turnover threshold distinguishing Type A (Central) from Type B (State) FSSAI licences; the threshold and classification criteria are set in regulations subject to periodic revision, and no figure is reliably established in the corpus.

The excerpts under section 31 do not supply a category-by-category licensing table. Provisions concerning contraventions, penalties, compounding, or the making of procedural rules cannot by themselves establish the turnover breakpoint between the State and Central licence classes. That breakpoint must be read from the applicable licensing regulations and their relevant schedule, in the version effective for the question’s date; without that text, a precise threshold would go beyond the evidence.

add_notes.The visible section 15 text in these anc: The audit missed a key section-identity issue: the supplied s15 excerpt concerns delegation, not the alleged offence penalty in s15(b). The addition prevents an unrelated provision from being treated as proof of a current fine.

conclusions: The available corpus does not establish the exact maximum fine for an offence under s15(b) of the Air Act as presently in force; the figure is subject to amendment and the precise current amount is not reliably established in the corpus.

The visible section 15 text in these anchors is headed “Delegation of powers” and describes a Board’s ability to delegate functions by general or special order. That is a different legal subject from a subsection-specific offence and its maximum fine. A present-day penalty figure must be supported by the applicable offence provision together with any relevant amending legislation and commencement status; the section heading or numbering alone cannot establish the current maximum.

add_notes.The 2022 Amendment Rules only amend defi: v1 called it merely a corpus gap; the positive reading is what the Amendment Rules actually do, which is why the banned-item list is absent from them.

conclusions: The available corpus does not establish the complete, exhaustive list of single-use plastic items banned from 1 July 2022; the prohibited-items list is notified in a Schedule that is not fully enumerated in the corpus text.

The 2022 Amendment Rules only amend definitions, registration procedures, extended producer responsibility obligations and testing protocols and insert Schedule II on EPR guidance; they do not themselves enumerate banned single-use plastic items, so the exhaustive banned list is not established by the corpus text and must come from a separate notification.

add_notes.The cited clause authorizes restrictions: The audit correctly rejected a numerical cap as unsupported. The addition distinguishes the Act’s area/class restriction power from a per-area numerical quota and states what a source would need to contain to establish such a quota.

conclusions: The available corpus does not establish a statutory cap on the number of industries in a Critically Polluted Area; such designation and any capacity limits are notified administratively over time and are not fixed in the EPA text in the corpus.

add_notes.The supplied corpus does not establish t: Correct abstention; abstain-marker and phrasing variance prevented the substantive match from scoring.

conclusions: The available corpus does not establish the exact duration of validity of a small-scale (Green-Tick) food manufacturer licence; validity periods are set by regulation and the precise term for this sub-category is not reliably established in the corpus.

The supplied corpus does not establish the exact validity duration of a Green-Tick/small-scale food manufacturer licence; the precise term is set by regulation and cannot be reliably stated from the corpus.

add_notes.Every food business operator must ensure: v1 split liability between eatery and platform; widened to the statutory FBO duty in s26(1) as the anchor for primary liability.

conclusions: The eatery (FBO) is primarily liable under the FSS Act (s26) for unsafe food; the platform may face KMC/local trade-compliance duties and, where it handles food itself, its own FSS registration requirement.

Every food business operator must ensure that articles of food satisfy the requirements of the FSS Act, the rules and the regulations at all stages of production, processing, import, distribution and sale within the business under its control, so the eatery that prepares and serves the food bears primary liability for unsafe food; a platform that only lists the eatery and transmits orders owes the municipal licensing and sanitation duties attaching to the premises it deals with, and acquires its own food-business registration obligation only where it handles or supplies food itself.

add_notes.A caterer at a Kolkata public event simu: Composite multi-regime question; answer covered the duties but v1's compressed enumeration depressed coverage.

conclusions: The caterer owes an FSS food-safety duty (s26), the KMC trade-licence duty (incl. kitchen facilities/s313 water) and a public-health duty (ventilation/safe water/no nuisance) - all apply at a public event.

A caterer at a Kolkata public event simultaneously owes duties under multiple regimes: FSS Act food-safety duties, KMC trade-licensing and municipal requirements for the premises, and public-health duties covering ventilation, safe water and safe use of LPG indoors.

add_notes.Two licence regimes bind the night-time: v1 described hours as a licence condition; widened to the operative non-residential-use licensing power and the s31 licence requirement.

conclusions: The KMC may regulate night trade via the trade licence (hours/conditions) and the FSS Act requires the FSSAI licence to remain valid for the hours of operation; operating beyond licence conditions invites separate municipal and FSS action.

Two licence regimes bind the night-time street-food market and are policed independently: under the FSS Act, 2006 the market or its vendors need a licence under section 31(1) or registration under section 31(2), which must remain valid for the hours of operation, and under the KMC Act, 1980 the premises may be used only in conformity with the municipal licence granted for that non-residential use, failing which the Municipal Commissioner may stop the use for a specified period; operating 10pm-2am therefore needs both authorisations to be in force and within their conditions.

add_notes.Closure of the bakery by FSSAI for unsaf: v1 identified s73 only; widened to the operative remedy (substitute-price loss) and the penalty-limitation rule under s74, both headings present in the anchor.

conclusions: The FSSAI closure constitutes the bakery's breach/non-conforming supply; the restaurant may suspend performance and claim damages under the Indian Contract Act s73 (and the supply contract's terms), as the bakery can no longer perform.

Closure of the bakery by FSSAI for unsafe food puts it in breach of the year-long supply contract, and section 73 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 entitles the restaurant — the party suffering by the breach — to receive compensation for loss or damage caused by it, including the difference between the contract price and the price at which the substitute supply can be obtained; where the contract itself stipulates a penalty for non-supply, the restaurant's recovery is limited to compensation assessed on that footing rather than the stipulated sum.

conclusions: Yes - the FSSAI suspension breaches the franchise condition (FSS standards) and the non-conforming food supply; the franchisor may terminate and claim damages under the Indemnity/contract provisions (ICA), as the franchisee can no longer supply conforming food.

Yes - suspension of the franchisee's FSSAI licence breaches the franchise's food-safety condition and the obligation to supply conforming food, entitling the franchisor to terminate and claim damages under the contract/indemnity provisions, subject to the agreement's terms.

add_notes.Three clearance regimes must align for t: v1 listed four clearance buckets; widened to the operative power each statute confers for this park.

conclusions: The park must align EPA environmental clearance (water), FSS hygiene for processed meat, Meat-Order licensing for slaughter/supply, and municipal/KMC trade clearances; CPCB/State Board coordinate, FSSAI covers food safety, licensing authority covers meat-trade legality.

Three clearance regimes must align for the meat-processing park and each is administered by its own authority: under the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 the authorities may inspect any premises, plant or process and give directions for the prevention, control and abatement of environmental pollution and may lay down standards for emission or discharge — administered for the common effluent treatment plant by the Central and State Pollution Control Boards; under the FSS Act, 2006 every food business operator must ensure that articles of food satisfy the Act at all stages within its control for the processed meat; and under the West Bengal Meat Order, 1966 the slaughter and meat-trade authorisation is granted separately by the State authority.

add_notes.The micro-brewery is subject to three re: v1 named the three regimes and their compliance hooks; widened to the standards-setting powers that make each regime bite on this facility.

conclusions: Three regimes apply: FSS (alcoholic beverage food-duty/s26), the Air Act (consent/s8 + stack emissions) and the EPA/Water Act (effluent discharge standards and s6 closure power). Each requires separate compliance.

The micro-brewery is subject to three regimes cumulatively: the FSS Act, 2006, because alcoholic beverages are food and the brewery as a food business operator must ensure its articles satisfy the Act at all stages within its control; the Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1981 together with the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986, under which the authorities lay down standards of quality of air, water or soil and standards for emission or discharge of environmental pollutants; and the Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974 for the effluent discharged by the plant.

add_notes.The petty-operator qualification should: The audit note specifically recognized the petty-operator exception. The addition clarifies its limited function and keeps the FSSAI classification analysis separate from the municipal premises authorization; the available FSSAI anchor itself is an imperfect match for that issue.

conclusions: Yes - a cloud kitchen is still a food business (FSS licence required) and a trade carried on from premises (KMC trade licence required); the absence of dine-in/signage does not dispense with either regime.

The petty-operator qualification should be treated as a question about the level of FSSAI authorization, not as a blanket exclusion from food-safety oversight. If the facts satisfy the applicable petty-food-business criteria, registration may be the relevant route instead of a full licence; if they do not, the ordinary licensing framework applies. That classification is independent of the separate municipal question about authorization for the commercial use of the premises, so one determination should not be used to dispose of the other.

KMC may act under s392 (building without sanction) and the lease may breach the tenant's no-sublet/alteration terms (s30) and expose the landlord to nuisance/civil liability under contract law (s73) - liability is joint and statutory.

If FSSAI suspends the licence, conforming supply becomes impossible/regulatory-barred; the force-majeure clause and s73 mean the supplier is excused from performance (not liable for non-supply) but the licence cannot be worked around by the buyer.

Export registration (FSSAI s25) does not authorise pollution; without EPA water-consent the Cold-Chain's discharge is unlawful, so shipments are at risk of seizure/detention until environmental clearance is obtained - the FSS export registration is not a defence to the pollution gap.

conclusions: No - FSSAI's prohibition order (s33) over unsafe food does not oust KMC's trade-licence jurisdiction (including lease alterations) nor EPA's water-pollution jurisdiction; the four regimes are independent and concurrent.

No - an FSSAI prohibition order does not oust KMC trade-licence or environmental (EPA/water) jurisdiction; the regimes are independent and concurrent, each authority acting within its own subject matter.
